## Main results The corrected section of the main results: “We identified 61 molecules in TF (Table 1), including fatty acids and fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule. The most abundant TF compounds comprised 27 or more carbons.” These changes were made to reflect the updated identifications and improve the clarity that these are the molecules we were able to identify rather than a complete list of all components found in TF. The last sentence places the emphasis on the molecules of interest (i.e., those abundant in TF) rather than on the molecules we were able to identify. The original section of the main results: “We identified 63 molecules in TF (Table 1), including eight fatty acids and fatty acid esters, 13 unbranched and 36 branched hydrocarbons with one to five methyl branches. The majority (40/63) of the TF compounds comprised 27 or more carbons.” ## Figure 3 legend The corrected legend for Figure 3 is shown here: … "The abundant component (peak A) found in TF samples but not on the cuticle was a cholesterol-like molecule that insects cannot synthesize but must receive from their diet. Three molecules outside this window were found only in TF and not on the cuticle: *-tricosene, oleic acid, ethyl oleate (Table 1)”…. The original legend for Figure 3 is shown here: … “The abundant component (peak A) found in TF samples but not on the cuticle was cholesterol, a molecule that insects cannot synthesize but must receive from their diet. Three molecules outside this window were found only in TF and not on the cuticle: 7Z-tricosene, oleic acid, ethyl oleate (Table 1).”… ## Methods A number of changes were made to the section of the Methods, “Identification of trophallactic fluid hydrocarbons”. These changes were made to reflect the updated method for identification, the updated identifications and to improve clarity. This section of the methods is shown here in full with corrected sections in italics. “Characterization of branched alkanes by GC-MS remains a challenge due to the similarity of their electron impact (EI) mass spectra and the paucity of corresponding spectra listed in EI mass spectra databases. A typical GC-MS chromatogram (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) reveals the complexity of the TF sample. The workflow described here was systematically used to characterize the linear and branched hydrocarbons present in TF samples summarized in Table 1. The parent ion was first determined for each peak after background subtraction. Ambiguities remained in some cases due to the low intensity or absence of the molecular ion. Linear alkanes present in TF samples were localized using a standard mixture of C8-C40 alkanes. Then RI values were deduced for all compounds present in the samples based on their retention times (Figure 3-figure supplement 1G, red). To determine the number of methyl branches for alkanes, we examined the distribution of fragment ions in the spectrum by fitting their intensities with an exponential decay function and specifically looking for the fragment ions that do not fit to the calculated exponential decay function. From the experimental mass spectrum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C), the intensity of all fragment ions was extracted and fitted with the function (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E). Figure 3—figure supplement 1 clearly shows two different resulting EI mass spectra profiles: on the left a linear alkane corresponding to n-hexacosane (Rt = 34.69 min, MF C26H54); on the right, a monomethyl-branched structure most likely corresponding to 9-methylnonacosane (Rt = 43.29 min, MF C30H62) with two enhanced fragment ions at m/z 141 and 309 emerging from the curve. Extracting and fitting the fragment ion profiles first helped to discriminate between linear and branched hydrocarbons, but also to estimate the number of methyl branches. To confirm for each compound the number of carbons and branches obtained, we used Kovats retention index (RI) values in the NIST Chemistry WebBook (Linstrom et al., 2000). Based on the RI values for similar GC stationary phase from C15 to C38 hydrocarbons, six different curves of RI vs. number of carbons were constructed from linear to pentamethylated alkanes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F). To construct the curves, average RI values were taken of all hydrocarbons available in the database, with a given number of carbons and a given number of methyl branches. For example, the RI value of 2409 obtained for C25 and two branches is the average of 3,(7/9/11/13)-dimethyltricosane, 3,(3/5)-dimethyltricosane and 5,(9/11)-dimethyltricosane values listed in the NIST Chemistry WebBook for the same stationary phase. Those curves were used to check for every compound that, from the measured RI value and the number of carbons found, the number of ramifications found fit properly with the curves. Once the number of branches and the parent ion mass were known, the position of the different branches could be deduced from the fragment ion values. When ambiguity remained on the position of the branch or double bond, this is indicated with an asterisk in Table 1. The plot of experimental retention times for each compound as a function of the RI index closely fitted the plot using RI values given by NIST for the identified compounds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), bringing additional confidence to the identifications. Table 1 summarizes the proposed structures for hydrocarbons and other compounds detected in TF samples.” ## Figure 3—figure supplement 1 The corrected Figure 3—figure supplement 1 is shown here: ![Figure 3—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/51082/elife-51082-fig3-v1.jpg) The original Figure 3—figure supplement 1 is shown here: ![Figure 3—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/51082/elife-51082-fig4-v1.jpg) ## Legend for Figure 3—figure supplement 1 Changes were made to reflect the updated identifications, to correct typographical errors, and to improve clarity of the methods. Corrected legend (corrections shown in italics): … “(B–C) GC-MS Mass spectra of a linear alkane (C26, elution time 34.69 min, panel B) and a methylated alkane (C30, Rt 43.29 min, panel C). (D-E) Extracted MS spectra were fitted with an exponential decay equation with their proposed structure based on enhanced fragment ions (m/z 141 and 309 in the case of 9-methylnonacosane). (F) RI values vs. number of carbons extracted from the NIST Chemistry WebBook library, depending on the number of methyl branches: linear (black), monomethyl (red), dimethyl (blue), trimethyl (pink), tetramethyl (green) and pentamethyl (dark blue) alkanes. (G) Retention index values calculated for each compound listed in Table 1 are based on the elution time and RIs of a hydrocarbon ladder from C8-C40 (black) overlaid with NIST RI values reported in the NIST database for the identified hydrocarbons (red).” Original legend: … “(B–D) GC-MS Mass spectra of linear alkane (n-hexacosane at Rt 34.69 min, panel B) and a dimethylated alkane at Rt 43.29 min (C). Extracted MS profiles were fitted with an exponential decay equation (B, D). The proposed structure for the branched alkane based on fragments ions (141 and 309) is 9,20-dimethyl nonacosane (D). (E) RI values vs. number of carbons extracted from the NIST Chemistry WebBook library, depending on the number of ramifications: linear (black), monomethyl (red), dimethyl (blue), trimethyl (pink), tetramethyl (green) and pentamethyl (dark blue). (F) The black dots represent experimental retention times with the calculated RI index for all identified hydrocarbons of the TF sample. The red dots represent the experimental retention times and with their RI index for the linear C8-C40 alkane standard.” The article has been corrected accordingly.

claims.claim: 61 molecules were identified in TF (trophallactic fluid).
claims.source: We identified 61 molecules in TF (Table 1), including fatty acids and fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 which lists the identified molecules, and is explicitly stated in the corrected main results text.

claims.claim: TF contains fatty acids and fatty acid esters.
claims.source: We identified 61 molecules in TF (Table 1), including fatty acids and fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1 which lists specific fatty acids (e.g., n-Hexadecanoic acid, Linoleic acid, Oleic acid) and fatty acid esters (e.g., Ethyl palmitate, Ethyl oleate).

claims.claim: TF contains linear alkanes.
claims.source: We identified 61 molecules in TF (Table 1), including fatty acids and fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1 which lists linear alkanes such as Pentadecane, Hexadecane, Heptadecane, etc.

claims.claim: TF contains double bonded hydrocarbons.
claims.source: We identified 61 molecules in TF (Table 1), including fatty acids and fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1 which lists molecules with double bonds such as *-tricosene, *-pentacosene, *-heptacosene, etc.

claims.claim: TF contains branched hydrocarbons.
claims.source: We identified 61 molecules in TF (Table 1), including fatty acids and fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1 which lists numerous branched hydrocarbons such as 5-methylpentadecane, 7-methylheptadecane, 2,10-dimethyloctacosane, etc.

claims.source: We identified 61 molecules in TF (Table 1), including fatty acids and fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1 which lists a 'Cholesterol-like' molecule with molecular formula C27H46O at retention time 45.54 min.

claims.claim: The most abundant TF compounds comprised 27 or more carbons.
claims.source: The most abundant TF compounds comprised 27 or more carbons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by inference from Table 1 data showing that the most abundant peaks (indicated by peak IDs and higher retention times) correspond to molecules with 27 or more carbons.

claims.claim: The abundant component (peak A) found in TF samples but not on the cuticle was a cholesterol-like molecule.
claims.source: The abundant component (peak A) found in TF samples but not on the cuticle was a cholesterol-like molecule that insects cannot synthesize but must receive from their diet.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from Figure 3 and Table 1 showing peak A corresponds to a cholesterol-like molecule (C27H46O) present in TF but not on cuticle.

claims.claim: Insects cannot synthesize cholesterol but must receive it from their diet.
claims.source: The abundant component (peak A) found in TF samples but not on the cuticle was a cholesterol-like molecule that insects cannot synthesize but must receive from their diet.
claims.evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about insect sterol metabolism.

claims.source: Three molecules outside this window were found only in TF and not on the cuticle: *-tricosene, oleic acid, ethyl oleate (Table 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing TF composition to cuticle composition, as referenced in Figure 3 legend and Table 1.

results.result: The authors identified 61 molecules in trophallactic fluid (TF) using GC-MS, including fatty acids, fatty acid esters, linear alkanes, double-bonded hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and a cholesterol-like molecule. The most abundant compounds contained 27 or more carbons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 and C31-C46 collectively provide comprehensive chemical characterization of TF composition supported by Table 1 data. The identification of 61 molecules across multiple chemical classes is directly supported by GC-MS data with retention times, molecular formulas, and retention indices. The claim about abundant compounds having ≥27 carbons is consistent with the peak IDs and retention time data showing major peaks in the higher molecular weight range.

results.result: The authors identified specific molecules unique to TF versus cuticle, including a cholesterol-like molecule (peak A), *-tricosene, oleic acid, and ethyl oleate. The cholesterol-like molecule is notable because insects cannot synthesize cholesterol and must obtain it from their diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 are supported by comparative data between TF and cuticle samples shown in Figure 3 and Table 1. The identification of TF-specific molecules is based on differential presence/absence analysis. Claim C9 about insect cholesterol biosynthesis is well-established knowledge in insect biochemistry and appropriately contextualizes the finding.

results.result: The authors developed and applied a systematic GC-MS method for characterizing branched alkanes by using retention index (RI) analysis, exponential decay fitting of fragment ion intensities, and comparison with NIST database values to determine carbon number, branch number, and branch positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 and C22-C28 describe a methodologically sound analytical approach. The use of RI curves constructed from NIST data (C22-C26), exponential decay fitting to identify branching (C17-C18), and fragment ion analysis for branch position (C27) represents a systematic workflow. The acknowledgment of remaining ambiguities (C28) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. The method is well-documented with supporting figures.

results.result: The authors demonstrated their analytical method by identifying n-hexacosane as a linear alkane and 9-methylnonacosane as a monomethyl-branched hydrocarbon, with the latter showing characteristic enhanced fragment ions at m/z 141 and 309.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 provide specific examples validating the analytical method. The identification of n-hexacosane (C19) and 9-methylnonacosane (C20-C21) is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 3-figure supplement 1B-E. The use of 'most likely' for C20 appropriately acknowledges some uncertainty in structural assignment, which is consistent with the challenges described in C13-C14.

results.result: The authors validated their molecular identifications by demonstrating close agreement between experimental retention times as a function of RI and NIST database values for the identified compounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 describe an important validation step supported by Figure 3-figure supplement 1G. The close fit between experimental and reference RI values provides orthogonal confirmation of structural assignments. This cross-validation strengthens confidence in the identifications made using the fragment ion analysis method.

results.result: The authors corrected multiple molecular identifications from the original publication, including changing 4-methyltetradecane to 5-methylpentadecane, removing mellein, changing 7Z-tricosene to *-tricosene, and changing cholesterol to 'cholesterol-like', indicating increased uncertainty about exact structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 document substantive corrections to the original identifications. Comparison of the two tables reveals systematic changes, particularly the addition of asterisks to indicate structural uncertainty (C50) and the more conservative 'cholesterol-like' designation (C51). These corrections suggest the original identifications were overconfident given the analytical limitations described in C13-C14. The corrections improve scientific accuracy but raise questions about the rigor of the original analysis.
